#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Consumer Credit
Description: The G.19 Statistical Release, "Consumer Credit," reports outstanding credit extended to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, excluding loans secured by real estate. Total consumer credit comprises two major types: revolving and nonrevolving. The G.19 also reports selected terms of credit, including interest rates on new car loans, personal loans, and credit card plans at commercial banks. The G.19 also includes series that measure the terms of credit for new motor vehicle loans at finance companies.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Consumer Credit
Description: The G.19 Statistical Release, "Consumer Credit," reports outstanding credit extended to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, excluding loans secured by real estate. Total consumer credit comprises two major types: revolving and nonrevolving. The G.19 also reports selected terms of credit, including interest rates on new car loans, personal loans, and credit card plans at commercial banks. The G.19 also includes series that measure the terms of credit for new motor vehicle loans at finance companies.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research report: Consumer Credit — Federal Reserve Statistical Release G.19

**Research checked:** October 8, 2026  
**Publisher:** Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System  
**Canonical release:** [Consumer Credit—G.19](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/)

## Executive findings

**Your title and description are accurate.** The description closely matches the Federal Reserve’s own explanation of G.19. However, a complete catalog record should add several qualifications:

- G.19 is a **family of national aggregate time series and a monthly statistical publication**, not a borrower-level dataset.
- It measures **outstanding consumer credit and changes in that credit**, excluding loans secured by real estate. It is therefore **not a measure of all household debt**.
- Its monthly publication contains information with **different underlying frequencies**, including quarterly interest-rate observations and quarterly student- and motor-vehicle-loan memorandum items.
- Estimates are **revised and benchmarked**. Published growth rates and flows exclude certain statistical breaks, so they need not equal changes calculated directly from published outstanding balances.
- Its historical coverage, classifications, and source systems have changed substantially.
- Two recent developments deserve preservation attention: **sector and benchmark changes implemented in July 2025**, and the **announced transition away from the Board’s Data Download Program in 2026**. [1–5]

**Overall assessment:** G.19 is a valuable, long-running public statistical resource for understanding consumer borrowing and selected borrowing costs. Its greatest analytical risks are confusing it with total household debt, treating net credit flows as new lending, ignoring revisions and breaks, and interpreting national aggregates as evidence about particular demographic groups.

---

## 1. Dataset identity and suggested catalog description

| Field | Verified description |
|---|---|
| Official title | **Consumer Credit** |
| Release identifier | **G.19** |
| Responsible publisher | **Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System** |
| Resource type | Continuing statistical release and associated aggregate time-series collection |
| Geographic coverage | United States, national aggregates |
| Subject coverage | Credit extended to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, excluding loans secured by real estate |
| Principal credit classes | Revolving and nonrevolving |
| Principal measures | Outstanding balances; break-adjusted flows; growth rates; selected credit terms |
| Publication frequency | Monthly |
| Underlying observation frequencies | Vary by series; not all information is observed monthly |
| Seasonal treatment | Seasonally adjusted headline aggregates; not-seasonally-adjusted holder and credit-terms information |
| Currency and units | Nominal U.S. dollars; release tables commonly use billions, while FRED series commonly use millions; rates in percent; maturities in months |
| Access | Public release pages, PDF, machine-readable downloads, FRED, and historical archival resources |
| Revision status | Continuing, revisable estimates |
| Household/borrower microdata | Not part of the public G.19 release |

### Recommended expanded description

> The Federal Reserve Board’s monthly G.19 statistical release, *Consumer Credit*, provides U.S. national estimates of outstanding credit extended to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, excluding loans secured by real estate. It reports revolving and nonrevolving credit, seasonally adjusted aggregate levels and growth rates, break-adjusted credit flows, and not-seasonally-adjusted balances and flows by major holder sector. It also includes quarterly memorandum estimates for student and motor vehicle loans and selected credit terms at commercial banks and finance companies. Estimates combine regulatory reports, voluntary surveys, administrative records, and other sources and are subject to benchmarking, revision, and statistical breaks.

This supplements, rather than contradicts, your description. [1–3]

---

## 2. Who publishes and produces it?

### Institutional responsibility

The **Federal Reserve Board**, rather than the Census Bureau, CFPB, or a commercial credit bureau, is the authoritative publisher.

Production depends on a network of contributors:

- Federal Reserve reporting programs collect information from banks and finance companies.
- Federal Reserve Banks participate in collection and editing of some institutional reports.
- Board staff construct national estimates, benchmark them, adjust for discontinuities, and prepare the release.
- Other federal agencies provide regulatory and administrative information.
- Credit-union organizations and private-sector vendors supply additional inputs.

The Board’s performance evaluation identifies its Public Affairs Office as handling release dissemination. **FRED**, operated by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, redistributes the series and provides analytical and download tools; it is not the original statistical producer. [6–7]

### Important distinction

“Published by the federal government” does **not** mean that every underlying input is a publicly downloadable federal dataset. Some inputs come from voluntary institutional reports or proprietary vendors.

This distinction matters for reproducibility: analysts can reproduce calculations using published G.19 series, but generally cannot reconstruct the entire production process from unrestricted source-level data.

---

## 3. Authority, mandate, and statistical governance

There are three distinct layers of authority.

### A. Historical origin: consumer-credit regulation

The Federal Reserve states that it has been the primary producer of aggregate consumer-credit statistics **since 1942**.

Its original role arose from responsibilities under:

- **Executive Order 8843, August 9, 1941**; and
- **Board Regulation W, Consumer Credit**.

These are historical origins, not a sufficient explanation of the release’s present-day legal basis.

Collection of credit-terms information began in **1972**, at the request of the President’s Committee on Interest and Dividends associated with President Nixon’s wage-price controls program. [6]

### B. Contemporary monetary-policy and reporting authority

For the credit-terms surveys **FR 2835 and FR 2835a**, the Board’s supporting statement identifies:

- **Federal Reserve Act §2A**, codified at **12 U.S.C. §225a**; and
- **Federal Reserve Act §11(a)**, codified at **12 U.S.C. §248(a)**.

Section 2A establishes monetary-policy responsibilities concerning monetary and credit aggregates and the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates. Section 11(a) supplies reporting authority.

**The obligation to respond to these two surveys is voluntary**, despite the Board’s legal authority to conduct them. Other G.19 inputs, such as institutional Call Reports, have their own mandatory reporting requirements. [8]

Consequently, it would be misleading to say that every G.19 source is mandatory—or that a single statute specifically orders publication of a release called “G.19.”

### C. Information-collection and statistical accountability

Underlying reporting programs have Office of Management and Budget control numbers. The Board’s evaluation lists, among others:

| Reporting program | Identifier | OMB control number |
|---|---|---|
| Weekly selected bank assets and liabilities | FR 2644 | 7100-0075 |
| Domestic finance-company consolidated assets and liabilities | FR 2248 | 7100-0005 |
| Selected consumer-installment-loan interest rates | FR 2835 | 7100-0085 |
| Credit-card interest rates | FR 2835a | 7100-0085 |
| Finance-company questionnaire/survey | FR 3033p/s | 7100-0277 |

These identify **source collections**, not a single G.19-wide collection number.

The Board also publishes performance evaluations addressing requirements of **Statistical Policy Directive No. 3, section 8**. These are useful evidence of statistical governance, quality review, and dissemination practices. [6,8]

---

## 4. What the dataset measures—and what it excludes

### Revolving credit

Revolving plans allow borrowing up to an agreed limit, repayment, and further borrowing without a new loan contract for each advance.

- Credit cards account for most measured revolving credit.
- Other arrangements, including prearranged overdraft plans, can be included.
- Revolving credit may be secured or unsecured, but real-estate-secured loans are outside G.19’s scope.

**Revolving credit is not exactly synonymous with credit-card debt.**

### Nonrevolving credit

Nonrevolving credit is closed-end credit repaid according to a prearranged schedule. Additional borrowing requires another contract.

Major components include:

- Motor-vehicle loans;
- Education loans;
- Personal loans;
- Other eligible consumer loans, such as boat and recreational-vehicle loans.

**Nonrevolving credit is not exactly synonymous with auto loans plus student loans.** [2]

### Major holder sectors

The current methodology identifies five major holders:

1. Depository institutions;
2. Finance companies;
3. Credit unions;
4. Federal government;
5. Nonprofit and educational institutions.

These classify **who holds or manages the credit**, not borrower characteristics.

Historical releases contain additional or differently organized sectors. [2]

### Memorandum items

Student loans and motor-vehicle loans are reported as memorandum items. They are **subsets of consumer credit**, not additional categories to add to the total.

The motor-vehicle memorandum item covers passenger cars and specified similar light vehicles used personally. Its definition excludes boats, motorcycles, and recreational vehicles, even though some such loans can appear elsewhere in nonrevolving credit. [2]

### Important exclusions and absent dimensions

G.19 does not provide a complete account of:

- Mortgages and other real-estate-secured household borrowing;
- Household income, assets, or net worth;
- Borrower race, ethnicity, age, sex, or income distributions;
- State, county, or neighborhood debt totals;
- Individual loan records;
- Loan approvals or denials;
- Comprehensive delinquency, default, or debt-collection outcomes;
- A separately identified total for buy-now-pay-later lending.

These limits are crucial for policy interpretation.

---

## 5. Sources and estimation methods

G.19 is an **estimated statistical system**, not a monthly census of every consumer loan.

### Benchmark-and-indicator architecture

The Board combines:

- **Benchmark data:** comparatively comprehensive, lower-frequency measurements; and
- **Indicator data:** higher-frequency information used to estimate movements between benchmarks and beyond the latest available benchmark.

The documented method uses **proportional interpolation** to reconcile monthly indicators with benchmark totals. Recent months are extrapolated until new benchmarks arrive, at which point earlier estimates can be revised. [2]

### Principal source relationships

| Component | Main documented sources and methods |
|---|---|
| Depository institutions | Quarterly institutional Call Reports provide benchmarks; weekly FR 2644/H.8 information supplies monthly indicators |
| Finance companies | Periodic Finance Company Surveys provide benchmarks; FR 2248 supplies higher-frequency information |
| Credit unions | Quarterly NCUA Call Reports provide benchmarks; monthly data from America’s Credit Unions supply indicators |
| Federal government | Department of Education student-loan portfolio benchmarks and monthly administrative information; Perkins-loan estimates are interpolated |
| Nonprofit and educational institutions | Department of Education information concerning relevant student-loan holdings |
| Commercial-bank loan terms | FR 2835 and FR 2835a |
| Finance-company new-car loan terms | Experian’s AutoCount Risk Report |

The federal-government sector consists of specified student-loan holdings, not all federal lending to individuals. [2,6]

### Seasonal adjustment

Revolving and nonrevolving credit are adjusted separately. The methodology page describes annual re-estimation using a historical estimation window and an X-12-ARIMA procedure.

**Documentation caveat:** portions of the live methodology page retain older descriptions and sample counts, including examples referring to 2010–2011. Preserve these statements as dated documentation; do not automatically treat every sample size or software detail as a newly verified 2026 production specification. [2]

### Break-adjusted flows

Flows represent changes associated with economic and financial activity, excluding specified statistical discontinuities.

Such discontinuities may arise from:

- New source coverage;
- Methodological changes;
- Reclassification;
- Transfers of loans into or outside the statistical coverage.

Thus:

> **Published flow ≠ necessarily current published level minus previous published level.**

And:

> **Published flow ≠ gross new loan originations.**

Repayments and other changes in outstanding balances are part of the net movement.

---

## 6. Credit-terms series: interpretation and frequency

The October 2026 release includes:

### Commercial banks

- New-car-loan interest rates for **60-month** and **72-month** loans;
- Credit-card rates for **all accounts**;
- Credit-card rates for **accounts assessed interest**;
- Interest rates for **24-month personal loans**.

### Finance companies

For new-car loans:

- Interest rate;
- Maturity in months;
- Amount financed in dollars. [1]

### The averages are not interchangeable

For bank auto and personal loans, published rates are simple, unweighted averages of reporting banks’ **most common rates** during the specified reporting week.

For credit cards:

- **All accounts:** an account-weighted stated APR measure;
- **Accounts assessed interest:** a measure based on finance charges relative to the balances against which those charges were assessed.

Neither is necessarily the interest rate faced by a representative new applicant.

### Quarterly observations in a monthly publication

Credit-terms observations occur at specified quarterly reporting points. A monthly-looking download or table does not imply monthly measurement. The current release displays `n.a.` in intervening months.

Data pipelines should distinguish:

- A genuinely observed monthly value;
- A quarterly observation;
- A value repeated by a downstream transformation;
- A missing or not-applicable value.

Historical auto-loan terms also differ from current terms. Older 48-month bank-loan rates and discontinued finance-company series should not be silently spliced to newer series. [1–3]

---

## 7. History and major changes

| Date | Development | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1941–1942 | Consumer-credit regulatory responsibilities established; Federal Reserve becomes primary aggregate statistical producer | Institutional origin |
| January 1943 | Start of the familiar current monthly total-credit series distributed through FRED | Series start is distinct from program origin |
| 1955 onward | Periodic finance-company surveys | Benchmark infrastructure |
| 1968 | Current revolving-credit series begins in FRED’s release listing | Component histories differ |
| 1972 | Credit-terms collection begins | Interest-rate history has a separate origin |
| Early 1983 | Major review and revision of the collection and compilation system | Quality, scope, and reporting-burden changes |
| 1989 | Securitized consumer-loan pools added to total credit | Coverage change and series break |
| 1999 | Automobile and “Other” credit combined into nonrevolving credit | Earlier split lacked a suitable benchmark |
| 2003 | Federal-government and Sallie Mae student loans added | Important expansion of student-loan coverage |
| 2004–2009 | Sallie Mae privatization and subsequent holder-label change | Institutional classification is not constant |
| 2010 | FASB 166/167 accounting implementation shifts much securitized lending onto institutional balance sheets | Holder movements may reflect accounting rather than borrowing |
| 2011 | Publication of older finance-company auto-loan-term series ceases | Discontinued data must remain distinguishable |
| 2012 | Depository sectors combined; credit flows added across loan categories | Changes to classification and available measures |
| 2013 | Nonprofit/educational sector and student-/motor-vehicle-loan memorandum items added | Expanded coverage and useful subsets |
| 2015 | Finance-company auto-loan terms resume using a new source and methodology, with history back to 2008 Q1 | New series are not seamless continuations of old ones |
| June 2020 | Release shifts from separate on-book/off-book lines to combined owned-and-managed receivables | Presentation and metadata change |
| July 2025 | Nonfinancial-business sector retired; credit-union benchmark expanded | Recent coverage and level-break issues |
| 2026 | Board announces changes preparing for eventual DDP retirement | Download and preservation infrastructure changes |

Sources: Board history, methodology, announcements, revisions, and FRED release metadata. [2–7,9]

FRASER’s catalog also records historical title variants, including *Consumer Instalment Credit*. These are useful alternate titles for discovery and archival cataloging. [10]

### July 2025 changes require special attention

**Nonfinancial business:** The Census Bureau’s relevant accounts-receivable estimates had been discontinued in 2020, and balances in this sector had greatly diminished. The Board stopped extending this sector beyond 2019. Historical total balances retain the sector’s estimates through 2019.

The Board explains that much retail credit is now originated through financial-institution partnerships and is captured in financial-sector holdings. Therefore, the sector’s retirement should not be described as removing all retail credit from G.19. [2,11]

**Credit unions:** The benchmark was expanded to include secured personal loans previously absent from its construction. The Board estimated an increase of approximately **$69 billion** in covered outstanding credit and inserted a series break so historical published growth rates would not interpret the coverage addition as new borrowing. [12]

---

## 8. Timeliness, revisions, and quality

### Release schedule

G.19 is generally released on the **fifth business day of the month**, at **3 p.m. Eastern Time**.

Its main monthly reference period is approximately two months behind the publication month. For example, the **October 7, 2026** release reports **August 2026** consumer credit. [1]

### Revision causes

Revisions can result from:

- Late institutional reports;
- Respondent corrections;
- Reclassification of loans;
- New quarterly or periodic benchmarks;
- Revised administrative data;
- Re-estimated seasonal factors;
- Methodology and coverage changes.

Release tables identify preliminary and revised observations using markings such as `p` and `r`. Significant changes are explained through footnotes, revisions pages, announcements, and technical documentation. [1,4,6]

### Quality strengths

- Long historical record;
- National scope across multiple lender types;
- Comprehensive regulatory benchmarks for important sectors;
- Explicit separation of levels, flows, and growth rates;
- Public explanation of major changes;
- Accessible redistribution and archival systems.

### Quality limitations

- Some indicators and interest-rate panels are voluntary samples.
- Early estimates precede comprehensive benchmarks.
- Monthly volatility reflects both economic change and measurement limitations.
- No conventional observation-by-observation confidence interval accompanies the headline release.
- Private inputs limit full source-level reproducibility.
- Long-term comparisons cross substantial changes in financial markets, classifications, and accounting.

The Board’s performance evaluation explicitly discusses uncertainty about how much high-frequency volatility reflects true borrowing variation versus measurement error. [6]

### Buy-now-pay-later coverage

The technical Q&A states that coverage depends on the lender and accounting classification:

- Bank and credit-union lending is generally well captured;
- Coverage of newly established nonbank BNPL providers is more limited;
- G.19 cannot separately track BNPL originations and outstanding balances.

**Do not use G.19 as a comprehensive, separately identified BNPL measure.** [3]

---

## 9. Typical users and public benefits

The sources document monetary-policy uses and downstream federal statistical applications. Other user categories below are practical applications, not a verified census of users.

| User group | Typical use | Public benefit |
|---|---|---|
| Federal Reserve policymakers and staff | Assess household financial conditions, credit growth, and implications for spending | Better-informed monetary policy |
| Federal economic statisticians | Use loan-term information in household interest and financial-obligation calculations | More informative national economic statistics |
| Academic researchers | Study credit cycles, consumer borrowing, financial-market change, and policy transmission | Reproducible research and historical understanding |
| Banks, credit unions, and finance companies | Compare sector trends and borrowing costs | Better market monitoring |
| Journalists and educators | Explain debt and interest-rate developments | Economic literacy and public accountability |
| Consumer and student-debt advocates | Track aggregate borrowing and selected costs | Evidence for policy debate |
| Investors and forecasters | Evaluate macroeconomic credit conditions | Widely accessible economic information |
| Librarians and preservationists | Preserve a continuing record of household finance and statistical practice | Long-term access and institutional memory |

The reporting documentation specifically identifies uses in monetary-policy analysis and in Bureau of Economic Analysis household-interest calculations within the National Income and Product Accounts. [6,8]

### What advocates can responsibly claim

G.19 can support statements about:

- Growth or contraction of covered consumer credit;
- The revolving/nonrevolving composition;
- Changes in credit held by major sectors;
- Aggregate student- and motor-vehicle-loan balances;
- Selected borrowing-rate trends.

It **cannot independently establish**:

- Racial or income disparities;
- Predatory treatment of individual borrowers;
- Local lending discrimination;
- Household financial distress;
- The causal effect of a law or monetary-policy decision.

Those questions require complementary data and an appropriate research design.

---

## 10. Access, formats, archives, and infrastructure changes

### Main access routes

1. **Board release pages:** authoritative tables, narrative, notes, and dated releases.
2. **PDF:** preserves the publication’s layout and footnotes.
3. **Data Download Program:** preformatted CSV packages and an all-data XML/SDMX ZIP.
4. **FRED:** series discovery, charts, downloads, and programmatic access.
5. **ALFRED:** historical vintages where available.
6. **FRASER:** archival publications, historical title information, and related documentation. [1,5,7,10,13]

The DDP currently lists packages for:

- All outstanding-credit series;
- Seasonally adjusted consumer credit;
- Terms of credit;
- Major holders;
- Revolving credit;
- Nonrevolving credit;
- Credit flows.

### Preservation warning: DDP transition

The Board announced that the DDP’s **“Build Your Package” feature will be removed during the week of November 9, 2026**, in preparation for eventual DDP retirement.

The announcement directs users to FRED and XML downloads on release pages. It does **not** establish that every old URL, discontinued series, or workflow will remain unchanged. [1,5]

**Immediate preservation priority:** capture the full available collection, discontinued series, metadata, download specifications, and documentation before infrastructure changes.

### Historical observations versus historical vintages

These are different archival objects:

- **Historical observations:** past dates using today’s revised estimates.
- **Historical vintages:** values available to users at a past publication date.
- **Historical releases:** publication artifacts showing tables, notes, and contemporary classifications.

A preservation collection should retain all three where possible. ALFRED coverage must be checked by series; it should not be assumed complete for every G.19 series and every historical release.

---

## 11. Data-science guidance

### Core analytical safeguards

1. **Read units from metadata.**  
   Board tables may show billions while FRED provides millions.

2. **Separate annualized flows from monthly flows.**  
   An annual-rate monthly flow generally represents twelve times the monthly amount.

3. **Use published break-adjusted flows and growth rates.**  
   Directly differencing levels can turn a coverage change into a false borrowing surge.

4. **Do not confuse an annualized monthly rate with year-over-year growth.**

5. **Keep seasonal treatments consistent.**  
   Mixing seasonally adjusted totals with unadjusted sector changes can produce misleading comparisons.

6. **Treat balances as nominal.**  
   Inflation-adjusted, per-capita, or income-normalized measures require additional data.

7. **Respect observation frequency.**  
   Quarterly terms should not be treated as newly observed in every month.

8. **Do not add memorandum items to total credit.**

9. **Preserve vintage information.**  
   Forecast testing using today’s revised history can introduce look-ahead bias.

10. **Avoid causal conclusions from aggregate correlations alone.**

### Concrete units example

The October 7, 2026 release reports August’s seasonally adjusted outstanding consumer credit as **$5,196.8 billion**, approximately **$5.197 trillion**.

Its August total flow is **$99.4 billion at an annual rate**—approximately **$8.3 billion for the month**, not $99.4 billion newly borrowed during August. [1]

### Useful complementary datasets

- **New York Fed Household Debt and Credit:** debt and delinquency measures based on consumer-credit-panel information, including mortgages.
- **Survey of Consumer Finances:** household balance sheets and demographic distributions.
- **SHED:** household financial well-being and reported hardship.
- **Financial Accounts of the United States, Z.1:** broader financial-sector and household accounts.
- **CFPB datasets:** complaints and product-specific research.
- **BEA/BLS data:** income, spending, inflation, and denominators for normalized measures.

These are complements, not interchangeable substitutes; definitions and populations differ.

---

## 12. Preservation and cataloging recommendations

### Minimum archival package

Preserve:

- Dated release HTML and PDF;
- Full machine-readable downloads;
- Series identifiers, descriptions, units, and frequency;
- Seasonal-adjustment status;
- Preliminary/revised markers;
- Footnotes and missing-value conventions;
- Methodology and technical Q&A pages;
- Revision and announcement histories;
- Performance evaluations;
- Reporting forms, instructions, and supporting statements;
- Available vintages;
- Discontinued series and their replacement relationships.

### Recommended metadata

At minimum:

```text
publisher
release_identifier
publication_date
reference_period
retrieval_timestamp
source_url
series_identifier
series_title
credit_type
holder_sector
measure_type
unit
frequency
seasonal_adjustment
annualization
observation_status
vintage_date
coverage_definition
break_notes
discontinuation_or_replacement_notes
file_checksum
```

Store original files and a normalized analytical version separately. Retain publisher notes alongside any local transformations.

### Preservation risk assessment

| Risk | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Loss of current headline totals | Relatively low because of multiple dissemination routes |
| Loss of discontinued series or old download workflows | Material, particularly during DDP transition |
| Loss of historical vintages | Material unless explicitly preserved |
| Loss of methodological context | High analytical consequence |
| False continuity across classification changes | High analytical consequence |
| Complete reconstruction from unrestricted raw inputs | Generally not possible |

I did not verify a G.19-specific DOI, an exhaustive file manifest, a formal retention schedule, or a dataset-specific preservation service-level guarantee. These should remain open questions rather than assumed catalog facts.

---

## 13. Privacy, confidentiality, reuse, and citation

### Privacy and confidentiality

The public release contains aggregates, not identifiable borrower records.

Nevertheless, confidentiality varies among source reports:

- Most FR 2835 rate information is not considered confidential.
- Certain explanatory narrative information may be confidential.
- FR 2835a individual respondent information is protected as confidential commercial or financial information under **FOIA exemption 4**, as described in its supporting statement. [8]

Thus, “public G.19 aggregates” does not imply “public access to all underlying lender submissions.”

### Reuse

Board-produced federal statistical material is generally reusable as U.S. government work. However:

- Do not assign a specific Creative Commons license without evidence.
- Distinguish published Board aggregates from proprietary input data.
- Preserve third-party notices and applicable platform terms.
- Do not imply Federal Reserve endorsement of derived products.

### Suggested citation

> Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. *Consumer Credit—G.19*. Release dated October 7, 2026. Specify series, units, seasonal treatment, reference period, and retrieval or vintage date. https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/

For data obtained through FRED, identify both the original Board source and the FRED series identifier.

---

## Bottom line

**G.19 should be preserved as a statistical system, not merely as a spreadsheet of balances.**

Its public value comes from its long record, broad lender coverage, regular publication, and transparent explanation of revisions. Its meaning depends on classifications, benchmarks, annualization, seasonal adjustment, and contemporary footnotes.

# Risk assessment: Consumer Credit—Federal Reserve G.19

**Assessment date: October 8, 2026.**  
**Scope:** The Federal Reserve Board’s G.19 release, historical publications, downloadable time series, and underlying reporting programs.

## Overall assessment

**G.19 is more likely to change its access infrastructure and selected data elements than to disappear entirely.** The release continues monthly, important reporting collections remain authorized, and monetary-policy and national-accounting users provide strong institutional demand.

However, two concrete preservation concerns are already documented:

1. **Historical coverage was reduced in 2025:** the current time-series repository no longer populates nonfinancial-business-sector observations after December 2019.
2. **The primary download infrastructure is changing:** the Board plans to remove the Data Download Program’s custom-package feature during the week of November 9, 2026, before eventually retiring the DDP.

FRED, XML downloads, dated Board releases, and FRASER reduce the danger of complete loss. They do **not**, without a series-by-series audit, establish that every discontinued series, historical vintage, and metadata element will survive migration.

The ratings below apply your rubric’s thresholds—not a numerical probability of disappearance. A **High Risk** rating for reduced granularity therefore does not mean that the entire dataset is likely to vanish.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence supporting elevated risk

- **Retrospective removal of a data element:** In July 2025, the Board retired the nonfinancial-business sector. Its technical explanation states: “Our last data point is December 2019, and entries following this month will not be populated in the public repository.”
- Previously published estimates after 2019 had carried forward a roughly **$35 billion** benchmark because Census stopped collecting the relevant source information in 2020. Removing those estimates also changed historical total-credit levels beginning in January 2020. Break adjustments protect published growth rates, but the current historical levels are not unchanged.
- **Historical download access faces migration risk:** The November 2026 custom-package removal and eventual DDP retirement make continued access through existing workflows uncertain. [1–3]

### Evidence supporting a lower rating

- Nonfinancial-business data **through 2019 remain available**, according to the Board.
- The Board maintains dated releases from earlier years, including releases predating the change.
- Historical publications are also held by FRASER.
- There is no identified evidence that whole prior-year release files have been systematically deleted. [1,4,5]

### Selected rating: **Moderate Risk**

This directly matches **“some data elements … prior to the current year or cycle are removed.”** It is not **High Risk** because I did not establish removal of historical publication files. It is not **Gone** because substantial historical data and publications remain accessible.

**Important distinction:** The removal was transparently explained and addressed unreliable carry-forward estimates. That makes it a defensible statistical change, but still a historical-preservation issue.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence supporting continued availability

- The current release was published **October 7, 2026**, covering August 2026, consistent with the usual fifth-business-day schedule.
- The release index lists monthly publications from January through October 2026.
- The credit-terms reporting collection, **FR 2835/FR 2835a, OMB 7100-0085**, was extended for three years without revision in April 2024. The current FR 2835a form states that approval expires **May 31, 2027**.
- The Board is pursuing another three-year extension of **FR 2248**, the finance-company reporting program that supplies G.19 inputs. Its July 2026 notice proposes revision, not termination. [4,6–8]

### Evidence supporting concern, but not a higher availability rating

- DDP retirement could disrupt automated downloads and custom queries.
- FR 2248’s proposed extension and revisions require continued monitoring.
- These are not evidence that monthly G.19 collection or publication has stopped or been delayed. [3,8]

### Selected rating: **No Known Issue**

I found no documented skipped release, missed publication deadline, or qualifying ICR expiration in the collections checked.

**Qualification:** G.19 draws on multiple collections and administrative sources; this is not an exhaustive expiration audit of every upstream reporting program. The active credit-terms approval and finance-company renewal process are strong evidence of continuity, not a guarantee covering every input.

---

## 3. Data Quality

### Evidence supporting elevated risk

- **An actual reduction in granularity occurred:** the nonfinancial-business holder category was discontinued, including its post-2019 historical estimates.
- The Board explicitly identified the absence of a **sound substitute** for the discontinued Census benchmark.
- **Pending upstream simplification:** The July 2026 FR 2248 proposal would remove the off-balance-sheet securitization column, consolidate real-estate-loan items, simplify equity reporting, and revise descriptions, effective for the June 2027 reporting period.
- Broader staffing reductions introduce an emerging capacity risk, although a G.19-specific effect has not been demonstrated. [1,8,9]

### Evidence supporting maintained or improved quality

- In July 2025, the credit-union benchmark was expanded to capture secured personal loans previously omitted, adding approximately **$69 billion** in covered balances.
- The Board documented the change and inserted a statistical break so it would not appear as new borrowing in growth rates.
- A September 2025 DDP error generated flows before the relevant series’ actual starting dates. The Board corrected it the next day and explained that recent observations, PDF/HTML releases, and historical tables were unaffected.
- Monthly publication continues. The FR 2248 proposal does not itself establish a reduction in G.19 frequency or headline detail; real-estate loans are outside G.19’s scope. [2,8,10]

### Selected rating: **High Risk**

Under your rubric, **actual reduced granularity** qualifies as High Risk, even when the reduction is justified and other measures improve.

This rating is concentrated in a **small discontinued sector**, not a finding that the remaining credit totals have become broadly unreliable. **Moderate Risk** would fit the proposed upstream changes alone, but the sector discontinuation is already implemented. **Gone** does not apply.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence supporting institutional protection

- The reporting documentation explicitly identifies **Federal Reserve Act §2A, 12 U.S.C. §225a**, and **§11(a), 12 U.S.C. §248(a)** as authority for FR 2835/FR 2835a.
- Federal Register documentation identifies the information as valuable input to **monetary policymaking**.
- It also identifies use by the **Bureau of Economic Analysis** in national-accounting calculations. In the 2024 renewal, BEA submitted a comment strongly supporting continued collection.
- G.19 is identified by the Board as a **Principal Federal Economic Indicator**. [6,7,10,11]

### Evidence supporting vulnerability

- I did not identify a statute specifically requiring publication of a monthly release named **G.19**, prescribing its complete series inventory, or fixing its release date.
- The credit-terms surveys are voluntary.
- Other collections—such as household credit-panel statistics and Financial Accounts—cover overlapping subjects. They are useful partial alternatives, but not exact replacements for G.19’s scope, frequency, and loan-terms measures. [6,11]

### Selected rating: **No Known Issue**

This is the best fit under your rubric’s protection for data **required for implementation of a federal program**: G.19’s inputs have named statutory authority and documented monetary-policy and national-accounting uses.

**This is not a claim that G.19 publication is expressly mandated by statute.** Its precise publication format and individual series remain more discretionary than its underlying programmatic purpose. A stricter rubric requiring an explicit G.19 publication mandate would produce a less favorable rating.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

### Evidence supporting elevated risk

- In May 2025, Chair Powell announced plans to reduce Federal Reserve System staffing by approximately **10% over several years**.
- Board budget documentation describes alignment with the federal hiring freeze, voluntary deferred resignations, operational consolidation, and reduced spending on some IT-modernization initiatives.
- The audited 2025 financial statements confirm restructuring was underway, with **$16.26 million** in restructuring charges covering voluntary departures and some involuntary terminations; restructuring was expected to continue in 2026.
- Leadership remains politically contested: August 2026 Reuters reporting describes the Administration’s continuing effort to remove Governor Lisa Cook, stalled by courts and political resistance. This meets the rubric’s **threatened leadership change** criterion. [9,12–14]

### Evidence against High Risk or Gone

- A planned reduction of roughly 2,400 System-wide positions is **not evidence that 1,000 employees have already departed**.
- I did not establish a completed 10–39% workforce reduction, a 20% budget cut, or G.19-team-specific losses.
- The audited statements report total Board operating expenses of approximately **$1.192 billion in 2025**, versus **$1.170 billion in 2024**—not an overall spending collapse. Spending is not identical to a budget appropriation, but it provides useful counterevidence.
- The user-suggested USAJobs tracker measures **job advertisements, not staff losses**, excludes positions not advertised through USAJobs, and announces that collection stopped December 31, 2025. It cannot establish current G.19 staffing. [12,15]

### Selected rating: **Moderate Risk**

The **threatened leadership change** meets your Moderate Risk criterion. Implemented restructuring and the planned 10% reduction reinforce the concern.

I would **not** assign High Risk based on the announced System-wide reduction alone: doing so would confuse planned departures with completed losses and System staffing with the Board’s G.19 production team.

---

## 6. Policy

### Evidence supporting Moderate Risk

- **Pending reporting changes:** The July 2026 Federal Register proposal would revise FR 2248, a direct G.19 source collection, beginning in June 2027.
- **Announced dissemination changes:** Custom DDP package building is scheduled for removal in November 2026, with eventual DDP retirement.
- These are identifiable proposed or planned changes affecting the dataset’s production environment and access. [3,8]

### Evidence against High Risk

- I found no evidence that the FR 2248 revision is a **Presidential Action-driven ICR**.
- The proposed rationale is reducing respondent burden and removing outdated or redundant fields.
- The 2025 sector retirement is attributed to changed lending practices and a Census source discontinuation dating to **2020**, not demonstrated political suppression.
- There is no identified negative policy notice denouncing G.19 or announced Administration directive to terminate it.
- Political conflict over Federal Reserve leadership and interest rates does not, by itself, demonstrate interference with G.19 statistics. [1,8,14]

### Selected rating: **Moderate Risk**

The pending FR 2248 changes satisfy the rubric’s proposed-change criterion. **No Known Issue** would overlook those changes. **High Risk** would require evidence of the specified Administration-driven intervention that I did not find.

---

## Preservation priorities

1. **Archive the full DDP collection before November 2026**, including discontinued series and metadata.
2. Preserve **pre- and post-July 2025 vintages**, not just today’s revised history.
3. Check migration parity across **DDP, release-page XML, and FRED**, particularly for discontinued series and footnotes.
4. Monitor FR 2248’s final approval and June 2027 implementation.
5. Obtain G.19-team staffing information before interpreting System-wide cuts as production losses.
